lesson.title: Places after the point
lesson.body: After the decimal point come tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. In 4.582 the 5 is 5 tenths, the 8 is 8 hundredths and the 2 is 2 thousandths.

lesson.title: Zeros hold places
lesson.body: Twelve and forty-five thousandths is 12.045, not 12.45. Thousandths need three digits after the point, so a 0 holds the tenths place.

lesson.title: Compare place by place
lesson.body: Line the numbers up at the point and compare from the left: ones, then tenths, then hundredths. 0.45 is greater than 0.405, because after the 4 tenths it has 5 hundredths and 0.405 has none. More digits does not mean bigger.

lesson.title: Only the next digit matters
lesson.body: To round, look only at the digit just after the place you keep. 5 or more rounds up; less than 5 leaves the kept digits as they are.

lesson.title: Line up the points
lesson.body: Write the numbers so their decimal points line up, then add or subtract place by place. Fill empty places with zeros: to take 2.35 from 7, write 7 as 7.00.

lesson.title: Check by estimating
lesson.body: 7 − 2.35 should be a little less than 5. An answer like 5.35 or 0.465 means something slipped.

lesson.title: Moving the point
lesson.body: Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 moves the decimal point 1, 2 or 3 places to the right: 4.56 × 100 = 456. Multiplying by 0.1, 0.01 or 0.001 moves it to the left: 37.2 × 0.01 = 0.372.

lesson.title: Count the places
lesson.body: Multiply as if there were no points, then count the decimal places in both numbers together. The answer has that many places.

lesson.title: Dividing moves the point too
lesson.body: Dividing by 10, 100 or 1000 moves the decimal point to the left: 45.6 ÷ 100 = 0.456. Dividing by 0.1 moves it to the right, the same as multiplying by 10.

lesson.title: Make the divisor whole
lesson.body: To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by 10 (or 100) until the divisor is a whole number. The answer does not change: 12 ÷ 0.4 is the same as 120 ÷ 4.

lesson.title: Find the question first
lesson.body: Read to the end to see what is asked, then decide which numbers you need. Some numbers in a problem are there only to distract you.

lesson.title: Check it makes sense
lesson.body: A share is smaller than the total. A number of pieces is a whole number. If an answer breaks a rule like that, go back a step.

templates.construct: Value of a digit from its place, to thousandths

formats.prompt: In {fmt(n)}, what is the value of the digit {g}?
What is the {g} worth in {fmt(n)}?
{fmt(n)} = {w} + {p == 1 ? '?' : fmt(d1 / 10)} + {p == 2 ? '?' : fmt(d2 / 100)} + {p == 3 ? '?' : fmt(d3 / 1000)}. What number goes where the ? is?

hints: After the point the places are tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.
In {fmt(n)}, the {g} is in the {place} place.
{g} {count} is {g} ÷ {tenPow}.
templates.explain: The {g} is in the {place} place, so it is worth {fmt(answer)}.

distractors.feedback: {fmt(value)} is the digit itself. What a digit is worth depends on its place, and this {g} is in the {place} place.
{fmt(value)} is what the {g} would be worth one place further left. Count again from the point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
{fmt(value)} is what the {g} would be worth one place further right. Count again from the point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

templates.construct: Write a decimal read in words, holding empty places with zeros

formats.prompt: Write as a decimal: {words(w)} and {words(f)} {count}.

hints: The word 'and' marks the decimal point.
Write {place} with {p} digit{p == 1 ? '' : 's'} after the point.
So {f} {count} is {fmt(f / tenPow)}.

distractors.feedback: {fmt(value)} puts {f} straight after the point. For {place} there must be {p} digits after the point, so zeros fill the empty places first.
{fmt(value)} has one place too many after the point. {f} {count} uses exactly {p}.

hints: Read the decimal aloud: {fmt(n / tenPow)} is {n} {place}.
So it is {n}/{tenPow} before simplifying.
Divide the top and the bottom by {g}.
steps: {n} and {tenPow} can both be divided by {g}

distractors.feedback: {frac(value)} reads {fmt(n / tenPow)} as {n} {p == 1 ? 'ones' : p == 2 ? 'tenths' : 'hundredths'}. It has {p} place{p == 1 ? '' : 's'} after the point, so it is {n}/{tenPow}.
{frac(value)} has a bottom number ten times too big. {fmt(n / tenPow)} has {p} place{p == 1 ? '' : 's'} after the point, so it is {n}/{tenPow}.

templates.construct: Write a fraction as a terminating decimal

formats.prompt: Write {num}/{den} as a decimal.

hints: A fraction is a division: {num} ÷ {den}.
Or change the bottom to {target}: multiply the top and the bottom by {scale}.
{num}/{den} = {num * scale}/{target}, which is {num * scale} {place}.

distractors.feedback: {fmt(value)} writes {num} and {den} with a point between them. A fraction means {num} ÷ {den}.
{fmt(value)} would be {num}/{numDot}. Here the bottom is {den}, so change it to {target} first.

templates.construct: Compare decimals place by place, not by how many digits they have

formats.prompt: Which number is the greatest?
Four bags of rice were weighed, in kilograms. Which bag is the heaviest?
Four children threw a ball. The distances are in metres. Which throw went farthest?

hints: Line the numbers up at the point and compare from the left.
All four have the same whole number. Compare the tenths first, then the hundredths.
Only one of them has {x} tenth{x == 1 ? '' : 's'} and {y} hundredth{y == 1 ? '' : 's'}.

distractors.feedback: {fmt(value)} has more digits, but that does not make it bigger. Its hundredths digit is 0, and {fmt(a)} has {y} hundredth{y == 1 ? '' : 's'}.
{fmt(value)} has the same tenths as {fmt(a)}, so look at the hundredths: {fmt(a)} has {y} more.
{fmt(value)} has 0 tenths, so it is the smallest of the four, not the greatest.

Now compare each choice with them, place by place.

{fmt(value)} is more than {fmt(hi)}, so it is not between them.

hints: The nearest {place} keeps {p} digit{p == 1 ? '' : 's'} after the point.
Look only at the digit just after that one: {next}.
{next} is {next >= 5 ? '5 or more, so the last kept digit goes up by 1' : 'less than 5, so the kept digits stay as they are'}.
steps: Keep {p} digit{p == 1 ? '' : 's'} after the point in {fmt(n)}
The next digit is {next}, so {next >= 5 ? 'round up' : 'leave the kept digits as they are'}

templates.construct: Add decimals with different numbers of places by lining up the points

formats.prompt: {fmt(a)} + {fmt(b)} = ?

Write {fmt(b)} as {fixed(b, pa)} so both numbers have {pa} places.
Now add {fixed(a, pa)} and {fixed(b, pa)} place by place, carrying as usual.
templates.explain: With the points lined up, {fixed(a, pa)} + {fixed(b, pa)} = {fmt(answer)}.

distractors.feedback: {fmt(value)} lines up the last digits, so {fmt(b)} was added as if it were {fmt((w2 * 10 + f2) / aPow)}. Line up the points instead.
{fmt(value)} adds the {f2} as if it were {f2} {pa == 2 ? 'hundredths' : 'thousandths'}. In {fmt(b)}, the {f2} is {f2} tenths.

templates.construct: Subtract a decimal of up to four places from a whole number

formats.prompt: A rope is {a} m long. {fmt(b)} m is cut off. How much rope is left?

Or count up: from {fmt(b)} to {w2 + 1}, then from {w2 + 1} to {a}.
{fmt(b)} to {w2 + 1} is {fmt(w2 + 1 - b)}, and {w2 + 1} to {a} is {a - w2 - 1}.
steps: {fmt(b)} up to {w2 + 1} is {fmt(w2 + 1 - b)}; {w2 + 1} up to {a} is {a - w2 - 1}

formats.prompt: A store has {fmt(total)} kg of rice. It sells {fmt(s1)} kg in the morning and {fmt(s2)} kg in the afternoon. How many kilograms are left?

Then take {fmt(s1 + s2)} from {fmt(total)}.

formats.prompt: {fmt(a)} × {fmt(b)} = ?
A strip of cloth is {fmt(a)} m long and {fmt(b)} m wide. What is its area in square metres?

hints: Multiply as if there were no points: {ai} × {bi}.
{ai} × {bi} = {ai * bi}.
{fmt(a)} has {pa} decimal place{pa == 1 ? '' : 's'} and {fmt(b)} has 1, so the answer has {pa + 1}.
